lines.name: Level: B2 · Topic: The Space Station

lines.text:
Living in Zero Gravity — Life on the International Space Station

The International Space Station (ISS) orbits Earth at approximately 28,000 kilometres per hour, completing a full orbit every ninety minutes. At any given moment, six to seven astronauts live and work inside this extraordinary laboratory, conducting experiments that cannot be performed anywhere else — because nowhere else offers permanent weightlessness.

The station is assembled from interconnected modules — pressurised cylinders where the crew lives and works. An airlock allows astronauts to exit for spacewalks without depressurising the entire station. A docking port receives visiting spacecraft that bring supplies and crew. The cupola — a dome of windows on the underside — provides a panoramic view of Earth and is the station's most photographed location. A truss — a long metal backbone — supports the solar arrays that generate electricity. Radiator panels dissipate excess heat into space. Antennas maintain communication with mission control. A hatch connects each module to the next.

Spacesuits are worn outside the station. A helmet protects the head and provides oxygen. A visor shields the eyes from unfiltered sunlight. Gloves allow dexterity for repairs. Boots anchor to the station's exterior. A tether clips the astronaut to the structure — without it, a drift into space would be irreversible. A jet pack provides emergency propulsion. A tool belt holds wrenches and other instruments. An oxygen tank supplies breathable air. A communication headset connects to the crew inside.

Daily life is adapted to weightlessness. Astronauts sleep in sleeping pods — small compartments with a zipped sleeping bag attached to the wall. The galley prepares food from dehydrated packets — water is added, and the meal is heated. A toilet uses airflow instead of gravity. A shower bag contains water for sponge baths. Velcro strips attach objects to surfaces that have no 'up' or 'down.' A laptop and a book float unless secured. A photo and personal items from home are stored in a personal locker. Exercise is compulsory — two hours daily on an exercise machine to prevent muscle and bone loss.

The science is the station's purpose. A microscope examines biological samples. A centrifuge separates substances in microgravity. A glove box — a sealed, transparent chamber — allows experiments with hazardous materials. A plant growth chamber tests whether food can be grown in space. A water recycler converts sweat, humidity, and urine back into drinking water. An air filter removes carbon dioxide. A spectrometer analyses materials. A sample container stores specimens. A data logger records measurements. An experiment rack holds equipment in standardised frames.

The control room on the ground communicates constantly. A control panel and monitor display the station's status. A keyboard, a joystick, and a radio keep the crew connected. A clock shows multiple time zones. A map display tracks the station's position. A camera documents activities. An alarm warns of depressurisation, fire, or toxic atmosphere.

The ISS is not a destination — it is a testbed. Every experiment conducted in orbit prepares humanity for longer journeys: to the Moon, to Mars, and beyond. The station proves that humans can live, work, and maintain their health in the most hostile environment conceivable — and that the knowledge gained there is worth the extraordinary cost of getting there.

lines.text: 'Astronaut' (from Greek 'star sailor') = used by NASA and ESA. 'Cosmonaut' (from Greek 'universe sailor') = used by Russia. 'Taikonaut' (from Chinese 'space sailor') = used by China. All refer to people who travel to space.

lines.text: The first Arab Muslim in space was Prince Sultan bin Salman Al Saud (Saudi Arabia, 1985). The UAE's Hazzaa Al Mansoori visited the ISS in 2019. Sultan AlNeyadi completed a 6-month mission in 2023. Guidelines exist for observing Islamic practices in space, including prayer direction.

lines.text: Many astronauts report a profound shift in perspective after seeing Earth from space — called the 'overview effect'. They describe borders disappearing and feeling a deep connection to all life on Earth. This concept appears in environmental and philosophical discussions.

lines.text: 'For' + duration: 'for six months', 'for a year.' 'Since' + point in time: 'since March', 'since the launch.' Present perfect continuous + for/since: 'They have been orbiting for six months.' 'They have been in space since March 15th.'

lines.text: Never combine 'most' with '-est': 'the biggest' (not *the most biggest). 'Most' + longer adjective: 'the most complex structure.' Short adjective + '-est': 'the biggest', 'the fastest.' At B2, this error should be fully eliminated.

lines.text: Modal + bare infinitive: 'must exercise', 'should maintain', 'can float.' No 'to' after modals. Alternative structures with 'to': 'have to exercise', 'need to maintain', 'are required to exercise' — these use semi-modals that take 'to.'

lines.text: 'Every' for regular intervals: 'every 90 minutes', 'every day.' 'Each' emphasises individuality: 'each orbit brings a new sunrise.' For frequency and intervals, 'every' is standard. 'Each' + singular works when highlighting distinct items: 'each module has its own function.'

lines.text: ✅ "Despite the extreme conditions, astronauts manage to live and work normally." / "Although the conditions are extreme, astronauts manage..."
lines.name: ✅ "Despite the extreme conditions, astronauts manage to live and work normally." / "Although the conditions are extreme, astronauts manage..."

lines.text: 'Despite' + noun/gerund (no clause): 'despite the extreme conditions', 'despite being weightless.' 'Although' + full clause: 'although the conditions are extreme.' Never 'despite + clause.' 'In spite of' follows the same rule as 'despite': 'in spite of the challenges.'
lines.name: 'Despite' + noun/gerund (no clause): 'despite the extreme conditions', 'despite being weightless.' 'Although' + full clause: 'although the conditions are extreme.' Never 'despite + clause.' 'In spite of' follows the same rule as 'despite': 'in spite of the challenges.'
